title: Low-rank approximation and Eckart–Young
subtitle: G2 lecture 053000 · baseline companion · needs expansion
adaptation: First-pass source-derived outline. Section excerpts and any vector equation come from the spoken lecture and its display-only mathematics appendix. Expand with worked mathematics, proofs and topic-specific diagrams.

slides.title: The problem and its setting
slides.lead: Suppose A is a linear map represented by a large matrix.
body: We would like to replace it by something simpler: a map whose outputs all lie in a space of dimension at most k. That is what rank at most k means. It is a constraint on how many independent output directions the approximation can use. We now want to choose the replacement that minimizes error. There are at least two reasonable ways to measure error. Operator norm asks for the worst error over all unit inputs. A second measurement adds up the squared errors over a complete orthonormal input basis.

slides.title: Rebuild the map one singular direction at a time
slides.lead: Let A map a finite-dimensional inner-product space E into another space F.
body: Let its positive singular values be sigma one, sigma two, and so on, in decreasing order. A has an orthonormal family of right singular vectors, and their images, after dividing by the corresponding positive singular values, form an orthonormal family of left singular vectors. For an arbitrary input x, A x is the sum of its contributions along these singular directions. The first contribution is sigma one times the coefficient of x along the first right singular vector, multiplied by the first left singular vector. The second contribution is the analogous term involving sigma two.

slides.title: Prove that nobody can do better
slides.lead: Take any other map B of rank at most k.
body: We cannot assume that B preserves the singular directions. It may choose any output subspace and may mix all the input coordinates. But its kernel has codimension at most k. The span of the first k plus one right singular vectors has dimension k plus one. Therefore that leading span and the kernel of B share a nonzero vector. Choose a unit vector x in their intersection. Since B x is zero, the error on x is A x. And since x is made entirely from the first k plus one right singular directions, the length of A x is at least sigma k plus one. Thus every rank-k B has operator-norm error at least sigma k plus one.

slides.title: Measure the total squared error
slides.lead: The operator norm looks at the worst unit input.
body: The Frobenius norm instead measures the sum of squared output lengths on an orthonormal basis of the source. Choose any orthonormal basis and apply the error map to each basis vector. Square each output length and add. A calculation with inner products shows that the sum does not depend on which orthonormal basis we chose. In matrix coordinates it is simply the sum of the squares of the absolute values of all entries. For the truncated singular-value expansion, use the right singular basis. Each retained direction has zero error. Each discarded direction with singular value sigma j has error length sigma j.

slides.title: Prove the squared-error lower bound
slides.lead: Let B be any rank-k competitor.
body: Call R its range, and let P be the orthogonal projection onto R. Every output of B lies in R. For any input x, decompose the error A x minus B x into two perpendicular parts. One part is the component of A x outside R. The other part lies inside R and equals P A x minus B x. The Pythagorean theorem says the squared error is the sum of the squared lengths of those two parts. It is therefore at least the squared length of the component of A x outside R. Apply this to every right singular vector and add. We obtain a lower bound equal to the sum, over j, of sigma j squared times one minus the squared length of P applied to the corresponding left singular vector.

slides.title: Work an example in both norms
slides.lead: Take the diagonal three-by-three map with diagonal entries five, two, and one.
body: Its singular values are five, two, and one. If we keep only the largest singular direction, our approximation has diagonal entries five, zero, and zero. The error has diagonal entries zero, two, and one. The operator-norm error is two, because the largest error on a unit input occurs along the second coordinate. The squared Frobenius error is four plus one, which is five. Its Frobenius norm is the square root of five. These answers differ because the two norms ask different questions. If we keep the two largest singular directions, the error consists only of the third diagonal entry. Both errors are one.

slides.title: What happens when singular values tie?
slides.lead: The truncated singular-value expansion is an optimal solution, but an optimal solution need not be unique.
body: Consider a map whose two largest singular values are both three. Suppose we are allowed to keep only one direction. The map treats that two-dimensional leading singular subspace symmetrically. We can choose different unit directions within it and obtain different rank-one truncations with the same optimal errors. When there is a strict gap between the k-th and k-plus-one-st singular values, the leading singular subspaces are more tightly determined.

slides.title: What to reconstruct
slides.lead: First, write out the truncated expansion and show that its operator-norm error is the largest discarded singular value.
body: Second, repeat the kernel-intersection argument against an arbitrary rank-k map. Third, prove the squared-error result using the projection onto the range of the competitor. Account for the fact that its rank may be smaller than k. Then derive the weighted-allocation bound instead of quoting it.
